title: What a vector database actually does

segments.text: Hey everyone, today we're looking at vector databases and why every AI app seems to need one.
Let's start with embeddings. An embedding model turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, a vector.
Texts with similar meaning end up with vectors that point in similar directions.
So 'cheap flights to Paris' and 'budget airfare to France' land close together even with no shared words.
To compare two vectors we usually use cosine similarity, which looks at the angle between them.
Now the problem. If you have ten million vectors, comparing the query to every single one is slow.
That brute-force approach is called exact nearest neighbour search, and it scales linearly.
Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour indexes instead.
The most popular one today is HNSW, a graph where you hop between neighbours to reach the closest points.
You trade a tiny bit of recall for searches that are hundreds of times faster.
Another option is IVF, which clusters vectors into buckets and only searches the nearest buckets.
In practice you also store metadata next to each vector, like the source document and date.
That lets you filter, for example only search documents from this year.
Here's a mistake I see a lot: people embed whole PDFs as one vector.
Long chunks blur the meaning, so retrieval gets worse. Split documents into chunks of a few hundred tokens.
Also keep some overlap between chunks so sentences on the boundary aren't lost.
Do you always need a dedicated vector database? Not really.
If you already run Postgres, the pgvector extension handles a few million vectors fine.
Reach for a dedicated database when you need huge scale or very low latency.
To recap: embeddings capture meaning, approximate indexes make search fast, and chunking matters a lot.
Thanks for watching, see you in the next one.

facts.fact: Approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW) speed up search
Chunk documents instead of embedding whole PDFs
pgvector in Postgres can be enough
